1.pericope_label: Joseph fell upon his father's face, and wept upon him, and kissed him

schools.summary: Gill describes the gesture exactly: Joseph laid his own face to the cold face and pale cheeks of his dead father, out of tender affection and grief at parting, which shows that he had been present from the time his father sent for him, through the whole blessing of the tribes and the orders about the funeral. Calvin sorts the chapter's grief into two kinds, this weeping flowing from true and pure affection while the Egyptian mourning that follows is more from ostentation and vain pomp, whence the proverb that the mourning of the heir is laughter under a mask; he will not censure genuine grief, and commends Joseph's filial piety, but warns that we need the rein, lest through intemperate sorrow we be hurried by a blind impulse to murmur against God.

Henry draws out why the grief was so heavy. Jacob was old and decrepit and must needs die in the course of nature, he was poor comparatively and a constant charge upon his son, yet such affection had Joseph for a loving father, and so sensible was he of the loss of a prudent, pious, praying father, that he could not part with him without floods of tears. From this he takes a rule, that as it is an honour to die lamented, so it is the duty of survivors to lament those who have been useful in their day, though for some time they may have survived their usefulness; and he is careful about what the tears can reach, since the departed soul is out of reach of them, but with them it is proper to show respect to the poor body, of which we look for a glorious and joyful resurrection.

Clarke repairs the join between the chapters, since the act appears suspended by the unnatural division of this verse from the preceding one, though we may rest assured it was the immediate consequence of Jacob's death. Wesley takes the kiss as an act of faith as well as of love, Joseph giving an affectionate farewell to lips already pale and cold, and supposes the rest of Jacob's sons did the same, much moved by his dying words.

themes: Joseph fell upon his father’s face, and wept upon him, and kissed him
natural grief and ceremonial mourning distinguished
the mitigation of sorrow sought in the hope of a future life

2.pericope_label: The physicians embalmed Israel, and the Egyptians mourned for him threescore and ten days

schools.summary: Gill puts the reason first, that the embalming was not merely the country's custom but a necessity, the corpse being carried into Canaan; he treats the art as a branch of medicine, citing Herodotus that the Egyptians had physicians peculiar to every disease and Homer that they were the most skilful of all men, and notes that the Septuagint renders the word instead as the buriers. Calvin grants that embalming with spices was in former times no fault, being a public symbol of future incorruption, but holds that where faith has not breathed its odour all embalming is vapid; he suspects Joseph conformed from fear rather than judgment, lest his father's condition seem worse than other men's, and says of the seventy days that the world affects to believe whatever is customary is lawful, so that what prevails carries along everything it meets like a violent inundation.

Clarke works from the words, the Hebrew for the men meaning the healers and the verb for embalming answering to an Arabic word of the same sense, also used of the reddening of leather, so that the principle may be analogous to tanning. He gives the process from Herodotus: the three wooden models at three prices, the brain drawn out through the nostrils with a crooked iron, the abdomen opened with a sharp Ethiopic stone, the belly filled with myrrh and cassia, the body salted with nitre seventy days, then washed and rolled in fine linen and given back to the relations, who prepare a coffin in the shape of a man. He reckons forty days for the process and thirty more lying in natron. Wesley says the art was practised so curiously as to preserve the very features of the face unchanged, and notices that many Egyptians, out of the respect they had for Joseph, put themselves into mourning for his father.

Ellicott doubts that the embalmers are meant, since they are not generally called physicians, and thinks the work was superintended by the physicians of Joseph's household; he confirms that Egyptian physicians were subdivided into classes each charged with a special disease, though Maspero thinks their knowledge inconsiderable, and adds that the practice ran from two thousand years before Christ to the eighth century after, the bodies so preserved being reckoned at four hundred and twenty millions. On the numbers he finds the sources at variance, Herodotus giving seventy days to the embalming but describing Thebes, while Diodorus agrees more nearly with the account here.

debates.question: How long did the embalming itself take?

positions.position: forty days for the process and thirty more lying in natron, seventy in all
somewhat more than thirty days, with Diodorus, the forty being included in the seventy of the mourning

themes: forty days for the embalming, seventy for the mourning
the Egyptian art of embalming and its purpose
whether a symbol of incorruption may be borrowed from the heathen

4.pericope_label: Joseph spake unto the house of Pharaoh: let me go up and bury my father

schools.summary: Gill observes that the words of dying men are always to be regarded by those who have any regard to duty and honour, much more when an oath is annexed, which among all nations was reckoned sacred. Calvin suspects a less creditable motive in the use of intermediaries, since nothing was less tolerable to the Egyptians than that their land should be despised, so that Joseph pleaded necessity and transferred the offence to his dead father; he was oppressed by servile fear, and that he could not move his foot without the king's leave shows him bound by his splendid fortune as by golden fetters. Calvin also notices what respect for an oath prevailed among blind unbelievers, since Pharaoh had not sworn and still deemed it unlawful to violate by his own authority a pledge given by another. On the procession he will not excuse the tumultuous clamour, and thinks even the seven days an excess, yet sees why God allowed it, since a private burial would soon have extinguished Jacob's fame, whereas now a sublime trophy stands before men's eyes.

Henry finds the fuller description of this funeral deliberate, since Jacob had spoken more than once of dying for grief and going to the grave bereaved of his children, and behold, he dies in honour, followed by all of them; the Egyptians who had looked on the Hebrews with disdain now knew them better, good old Jacob having so conducted himself as to gain universal esteem.

Clarke explains why Joseph did not apply in person, since he was in mourning habit and none in such dress might appear before an eastern monarch; he likens the elders of the house to the Aldermen of our Saxon ancestors, and sets the procession against a modern state funeral, since here was no conqueror, no mighty man of valour, no person of proud descent, but a plain man who had dwelt almost all his life in tents, with no subjects but his cattle, and the reason Joseph was so honoured was not that he had conquered nations but that he had saved men alive. Wesley reads the application to Pharaoh as simple respect, since though the charge about the corn was long over Joseph was still a prime minister of state.

Ellicott describes the mourner's state, the dress squalid, the beard unshorn, the hair in disorder, and the man expected to keep to his own house while those signs were maintained. Keil corrects the verb in Jacob's account of the tomb, which means to dig and not to buy, so that Jacob attributes to himself as patriarch what had really been done by Abraham, and notes that royal permission was needed because Joseph meant to go beyond the border with a large procession.

outliers.note: Holds that Joseph did not dare frankly to profess his own faith, and takes his dependence on the king's leave as a warning that nothing is better for men of sane mind than a private station.

themes: my father made me swear, saying, Lo, I die
why the request was made through the courtiers
a national funeral for a man whose kingdom was not of this world

8.pericope_label: They mourned at the threshingfloor of Atad, and buried him in the cave of Machpelah

schools.summary: Gill lists the company and the reasons for the escort, honour and grandeur on one side and safety on the other, in case they were set upon by robbers or opposed by the Canaanites and refused the cave of Machpelah; he reports the derivation of Atad from the thorns with which threshing-floors were hedged, and passes on Jerome's location three miles from Jericho and two from Jordan, called in his day Bethagla, the place of a circuit. On the burial he is careful that his sons carried him means they saw to it, not that they bore him on their shoulders as the devout men bore Stephen. Calvin asks why they all went back to Egypt, and thinks they were drawn less by the pledges they had left there than by the oracle given to Abraham, that his seed should be a stranger in a land not theirs; they returned because it was not lawful to shake off the yoke God had laid on their necks.

Clarke says the word means a bramble, so the Arabic takes it for a place though all the other versions and the Targums make it a man's name, and since threshing-floors were always in the open field, Atad was probably a great farmer or the chief of a clan. He turns the seven days into an argument, since Hebrew mourning was ordinarily seven days and by exception thirty, never longer, the seventy being Egyptian and forced by the embalming, whereas man has added eleven whole months, which nature itself pronounces absurd, so that mourning is now a grave mimicry and a vain show convicting itself of hypocrisy. He also notes that Locke and others would attach the two verses about the burial to the close of the previous chapter, where they read more consistently. Wesley takes the name Abel-mizraim as a standing testimony against the next generation of Egyptians, who oppressed the posterity of the Jacob to whom their ancestors showed such respect.

Ellicott notes that the word for the great company is properly camp, that the Egyptian elders were chief officers of Pharaoh's household and of the districts into which the country was divided, and that on the Israelite side only the men of rank went. He explains the route east of the Dead Sea, since the wilderness of Judah was difficult and the path above Engedi probably impracticable for chariots, while the easy Philistine road was unsafe, hostilities being recorded between the sons of Joseph and the Philistines. On the name he finds a play of the kind always dear to Orientals, the words for mourning and for meadow differing only in a vowel, so that the versions, made before the points were affixed, all read the mourning of Egypt where the pointed Hebrew has the meadow of Egypt. Keil thinks the Egyptian procession stopped at Atad, since only Jacob's sons are named as carrying him into Canaan.

debates.question: Is Atad a person or a place?

positions.position: a man's name, with all the versions and the Targums, probably a great farmer or clan chief
a description, the floor being hedged about with thorns as threshing-floors were

themes: a great and very sore lamentation at the threshingfloor of Atad
wherefore the name of it was called Abel-mizraim
how long mourning ought to last

15.pericope_label: Joseph's brethren feared, and sent a messenger saying, Forgive the trespass of thy brethren

schools.summary: Gill reads their seeing as an act of the mind rather than the eye, since they considered that their father was dead and buried, that they had lost a parent concerned for the peace of all his family, and that what turn things would now take they did not know; on the embassy he rejects the guesses that Bilhah or her sons were sent, and thinks the messengers were of their own number, likely Judah and Benjamin. Calvin presses the injustice of their fear, since they judged Joseph by their own disposition and imagined that respect for his father alone had made him postpone revenge, which wronged a man whose liberality had shown his mind free from hatred, and wronged God too, whose grace had shone in that moderation; he thinks the device of mediators foolish, since they might have done better in person, and takes their plea as a rule that where the bond of religion is added we are harder than iron if not inclined to compassion.
Henry says that a guilty conscience exposes men to continual frights, so that those who would be fearless must keep themselves guiltless.

Clarke takes the fear as evidence of guilt rather than danger, since conscience records criminality and, breeding continual fears, destroys all peace of mind, and quotes Juvenal in Dryden's version, that though bribes or favour pronounce a man guiltless, none quits himself, his own impartial thought will damn him. He will not decide whether Jacob left such a charge, judging the notion of a feigned story unlikely, since Jacob may have had his own suspicions and thought it best that his sons humble themselves. On the title they use he thinks the words wonderfully well chosen and spoken in the most forcible manner to Joseph's piety and filial affection. Wesley says that while their father lived they thought themselves safe under his shadow, explains that they were not only children of the same Jacob but worshippers of the same Jehovah, and distinguishes Joseph's tears as sorrow that they should suspect him and tenderness at their submission.

Ellicott renders the fear as a question, what if Joseph should hate us, and notes that they had seen no change in his treatment of them, only that if he cherished revenge they were now in his power. Keil finds the sentence broken off before its end, an aposiopesis presupposing a case not desired and for the present not real, though perhaps possible.

outliers.note: Denies that the scene was staged, holding that Joseph, learning from the messengers how their minds were tormented, sent for them, and that their own deprecating speech drew the tears.

themes: Joseph will peradventure hate us, and requite all the evil we did unto him
forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father
a guilty conscience as its own tormentor

18.pericope_label: Fear not: ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good

schools.summary: Gill notes that the messengers' return gave them courage to come from Goshen themselves, and will not let their intention be softened, since they meant to contradict his dreams, take away his life, or at least make him a slave all his days. Calvin sifts the readings of Joseph's question and rejects most of them, holding that it means a mortal may not presume to thwart the counsel of God, and that Joseph restrains his feelings as with a bridle. He uses the next verse to separate two things in one act, since the selling was a crime detestable for its cruelty and perfidy and yet he was not sold except by the decree of heaven; while the brethren contrived their brother's destruction God was effecting their deliverance from on high, and whatever poison Satan produces God turns to medicine for his elect. On the promise of maintenance he insists that solid reconciliation means not merely abstaining from malice but overcoming evil with good, since withdrawing our hands from help is itself a revenge.

Clarke allows the question to be either question or affirmation, so that either Joseph has passed the transgression by and the matter now lies between them and God, or he stands in God's place as a distributor of his bounty and will nourish them and their little ones. Wesley hears humility rather than office, Joseph thinking they showed him too much respect and answering as Peter did Cornelius, stand up, I myself also am a man; he admires the manner as much as the substance, since Joseph would not tell them they were upon their good behaviour nor hold them in suspense, and concludes that those we love and forgive we must not only do well for, but speak kindly to.

Ellicott takes the question as a refusal of the judge's office, judges being sometimes called God in Hebrew as exercising his authority, points out that the verb is the same in both clauses so that man's purpose is set against God's in one word, and identifies the great people saved as the Egyptians; on the little ones he notes that the word is rendered households by the Greek and families by the Syriac.

debates.question: What does Joseph mean by asking whether he is in the place of God?

positions.position: that he declines the office of judge, which belongs to God
either that the matter now lies between them and God, or that he stands in God’s place as dispenser of his bounty
that a mortal may not presume to thwart the counsel of God, so that submission to God is what bridles his anger
that he is himself only a man, and that they should make their peace with God first

themes: am I in the place of God?
ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good
he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them

22.pericope_label: Joseph lived an hundred and ten years, and saw Ephraim's children of the third generation

schools.summary: Gill sums the years quietly, that Joseph dwelt in Egypt comfortably and in great prosperity, and not he only but his brethren and their families as long as he lived; on the third generation he draws the conclusion that Jacob's prediction of Ephraim's greatness and numbers had very early begun to take effect. Calvin finds the constancy more remarkable than the length, since Joseph, raised to great honour among the Egyptians, remained closely united to his father's house and gradually took his leave of the treasures of the court, lest earthly dignity should separate him from the kingdom of God; he spent sixty years bringing himself and his children into a state of submission, imitating the serpents which cast off their slough that, being stripped of their old age, they may gather new strength, and would rather see his descendants devoted to a pastoral life and despised by the Egyptians, if only they might be reckoned in the family of Israel.

Henry reads the length of the life as a reward attached to a commandment, since having honoured his father Joseph's days were long in the land which for the present God had given him, and it was a great mercy to his relations that God continued him so long; he adds that it contributes much to the comfort of aged parents to see their posterity in a flourishing condition, especially if with it they see peace upon Israel.

Clarke measures the clause about his father's house forward, since it means all the descendants of Israel, who continued in Egypt until the departure under Moses and Aaron a hundred and forty-four years later; on the knees he takes the phrase practically, that the children were educated by Joseph or under his direction, his sons and their children continuing to acknowledge him as head of the family as long as he lived.

Ellicott makes the third generation Joseph's great-grandchildren and instances Eran, the son of Shuthelah and grandson of Ephraim, as one born in his lifetime; on the phrase about the knees he is careful, since the Hebrew says they were born upon Joseph's knees, which means that he adopted them, though they would not form tribes, that prerogative being reserved for the sons of Jacob, but would count as his sons and form families.

themes: Joseph lived an hundred and ten years
the children of Machir were brought up upon Joseph’s knees
a courtier weaning his sons from the hope of his own rank

24.pericope_label: I die: and God will surely visit you; ye shall carry up my bones from hence

schools.summary: Gill sets the scene, Joseph calling them together some time before the end and saying he expected to die shortly, and observes that the oath was taken not of the brethren only but of their posterity, as many as were grown, so that it might reach the generation that departed out of Egypt. Calvin asks why Joseph alone is recorded as leaving such a charge, and singles him out for two reasons, that the eyes of all were fixed on him for his high authority so that it was his duty to lead the way, and that it mattered as an example that the man who held second place in Egypt should be content with a portion which was only that of the heir of a bare promise. He then asks where the certainty came from, since no vision or angel is recorded, and answers that it came from his father, Joseph relying on Jacob's testimony as securely as if a vision had been given him — whence, unless the hearing of the word suffices for our faith, we do not deserve that God should deal with us. On the bones he hears an admission that the exile would feel like oblivion, and takes the choice of a sepulchre as a seal of redemption.

Clarke reads the promise as pointing past the present comfort of Egypt, since they have there everything that can make life comfortable but not the land given by covenant, which represents the rest remaining for the people of God; he traces the sequel of the oath, that their descendants held themselves bound, Moses took the body at the departure and Joshua buried it at Shechem, and reads the charge as Hebrews does, an act of faith made when dying, by which Joseph expressed his belief in the immortality of the soul and the resurrection. Wesley draws the pastoral use, that we must comfort others with the comforts wherewith we have been comforted of God, and that God's gracious visits make up the loss of our best friends; he sets the choice as a comparison, since in Egypt they buried their great men with much pomp, and Joseph prefers a plain burial in Canaan, deferred almost two hundred years, to a magnificent one where he lay.

Ellicott notes what the sentence accomplishes, being both the proof of Joseph's faith commended in Hebrews and the preparation for the next book, so that his faith joins the two. Keil notes that the body was laid in the ordinary coffin of sycamore wood and deposited in a room, as Egyptian custom required, where it stayed three hundred and sixty years until the exodus.

outliers.note: Uses Joseph's certainty, drawn from his father's teaching rather than from any oracle of his own, to restrain those who desire visions and despise the ordinary ministry of the Church.

themes: God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land
he took an oath of the children of Israel concerning his bones
faith resting on a father’s testimony rather than a vision

26.pericope_label: So Joseph died, and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt

schools.summary: Gill dates the death from several quarters, the age being the exact number assigned by Polyhistor out of Demetrius, a heathen writer, while the Jewish writers say Joseph died first of the twelve patriarchs though he was the youngest, and Ussher places it in the year of the world 2369. He describes the Egyptian practice of standing such a chest against a wall, thinks the body was most likely kept in Goshen in the charge of Joseph's posterity, and reports Leo Africanus placing the burial in the Heracleotic nome, from which Moses dug him up.

Clarke reads the Hebrew idiom, which calls Joseph the son of a hundred and ten years, as a personification of the period of life, all its years represented as a nurse or father feeding and supporting him to the end, the figure rhetoricians call prosopopoeia. He notes that the same precautions were taken as for Jacob and were particularly necessary here, the body having to last a hundred and forty-four years; and he treats the coffin as a mark of distinction, since with us the poorest have coffins and the parish pays if the relations cannot, whereas in the east they are not always used, and the ancient Jews seem to have buried without them. In Egypt they were used, and cases of stone and sycamore survive, besides those of cloth folded and glued many times and painted with hieroglyphics; but Maillet reports that most bodies were simply embalmed and swathed and laid side by side without ceremony, the niches being designed for heads of families, so that a coffin marks the honour the Egyptians did Joseph in death as in life. Wesley draws the lesson from the long delay, that if the soul does but return to its rest with God the matter is not great though the body find its rest late or not at all, yet care ought to be taken of the bodies of the saints in the belief of their resurrection, for there is a covenant with the dust which shall be remembered.

Ellicott says the word means a case or chest of wood, the mummy-cases being generally sycamore, and gives the reason for keeping the body near, since with their great protector gone the Israelites could not have gone up to Hebron with a military escort, so the embalmed body was to lie where it could easily be removed when deliverance came. He closes the book with a survey: in Palestine, where Abraham had wandered as a stranger, the family could never have multiplied, the peoples there being too powerful to permit it, so that Abraham and Lot, and Esau and Jacob, had been forced apart, whereas now under Joseph they were settled in a large, fertile and almost uninhabited region among men of their own stock, and when we next read of them they had grown into a people so vast that Egypt was afraid of them.

themes: he was put in a coffin in Egypt
a coffin as an Egyptian mark of distinction
the preparation for a nation ends with Joseph’s death
